title: Wooden Treasure Basket
strapline: Warm, smooth and full of grain — a basket of real wood for hands and mouths that want to know what wood is.
intent: Offer sitting babies the warmth, weight and honest grain of real wood — a whole material family plastic only imitates.
Strengthen reaching, grasping, mouthing and releasing on rings, bowls, spoons and dowels of different sizes.
Support long, self-chosen concentration — the baby decides what to bang, stack, dangle and mouth, and for how long.
Feed the earliest sound-making and knocking as wood meets wood — softer than metal, but wholly its own.
Keep a trusted adult close and calm, so the exploring happens from a place of safety.
implementation: Gather smooth, splinter-free wooden treasures: napkin rings, a small bowl, wooden spoons, a curtain ring on a cord, dowel offcuts, a wooden egg, bangles, a little brush with a wooden back.
Sit the baby steadily with the basket in reach and settle low beside them — attentive face, relaxed body, no 'look at this one'.
Meet the baby's gaze when they hold something up, name it softly ('the smooth ring — warm, isn't it'), and hand it back.
Follow the fascinations — more rings for the dangler, more bowls for the poster, more spoons for the banger — and refresh weekly.
Check every piece for splinters, cracks and loose finish before each session, keep everything larger than a choke tube, and oil bare wood with food-safe oil, never varnish.
key_questions: The wood is warm, not cold like the spoon — can you feel it?
What does the bowl sound like when the ring goes in?
You keep coming back to the little egg — what does it do that the others don't?
Which wooden treasure will you show me next?
Can you fit the ring over the dowel — nearly!

impact.text: Babies reach in, grasp the wooden treasures, transfer them hand to hand and mouth them to find out more.
Babies explore the wood with every sense — mouthing the ring, stroking the grain, sniffing the bowl.
A baby drops the egg to watch it roll, posts the ring into the bowl, and repeats the experiment again and again.
A baby taps spoon on bowl, listens to the softer wooden knock, and does it once more on purpose.
A baby holds the smooth egg up towards their key person and babbles — a real conversation over a treasure.
With their key person close and calm, the baby ranges across the basket and returns with a glance, not a cry.

enhancements: A cord of wooden bangles and rings for the danglers to swing.
Graduated wooden bowls for nesting, stacking and lid-matching.
A basket paired with a wooden mirror surround, so treasures and reflection meet.
Rolling wood only for a session — eggs, dowels, a rolling pin — and watch the rolling research begin.
A little wooden brush to stroke along a bare arm — texture for the whole body.

playing_exploring: The baby follows their own fascination through the basket, with no right way to play.
Wood is tested with hands, mouth and ears — real research with real material.
active_learning: Babies revisit the same treasure across days, concentration running long when no one interrupts.
creating_thinking: Babies predict what wood will do — roll, knock, fit — and show surprise when it behaves its own way.
